newsitem.title: UK: Feeling low? Take a red pill, study advises.
newsitem.headline: Feeling low? Take a red pill, study advises.

text.p: The colours and names of drugs strongly affect how people think they will work, researchers reported on Friday.

Peppy red colours make people think a stimulant will work, while calming blue actually does seem to send people off to sleep more quickly, epidemiologist Anton de Craen and colleagues at the University of Amsterdam found.
"Colours affect the perceived action of a drug and seem to influence the effectiveness of a drug," they wrote in a report in the British Medical Journal.
They reviewed 12 different studies on pill and capsule colours and found consistent effects.
"Red, yellow and orange are associated with a stimulant effect, while blue and green are related to a tranquillising effect," they wrote.
"Hypnotic, sedative and anxiolytic (anti-anxiety) drugs were more likely than antidepressants to be green, blue or purple."
They said the effects of colours had been seen across various cultures, and some studies showed that patients actually registered the effects of their colour prejudices.
"Patients taking blue capsules reported falling asleep significantly more quickly than those taking the orange capsules," they wrote.
A second study in the BMJ questioned whether drugs companies should be allowed such freedom and imagination in naming drugs.

Soren Holm of the University of Copenhagen and Martyn Evans of the University of Wales checked to see if the names of drugs truly reflected what they could do for people and found some "morally troubling" names.
"They often promise more than the drug can deliver," they wrote.

For example, many sleeping pills carried names implying a good night's sleep. "Given what is known about the long-term effects of such drugs, it is to say the least morally problematic to name them in such a way as to imply only the desired effects," they wrote.
Many sleeping pills create long-term dependence and can be very dangerous mixed with alcohol.
"Similar misplaced imagination can be found in the naming of antidepressants," they added.

"Are we really to believe that these chemical substances can help the depressed patient...get back up to full speed, see inner light, achieve inner harmony, brighten up (as some brand names imply)?" they asked.
They said regulators who approve drugs should do a larger study. "We think it would be reasonable to require that no drug with a misleading name should be registered for sale," they recommended.
